title: Review of Minimum Annual Leave Entitlement of Seven Days under Employment Act
what_it_is: Review of Minimum Annual Leave Entitlement of Seven Days under Employment Act

sections.label: Annual leave entitlement and statistics
sections.summary: The Employment Act sets a minimum of seven days annual leave, rising one day per year of service, and 2022 data show most full-time resident employees had more than seven days.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
sentences.text: While the Employment Act stipulates a minimum entitlement of seven days of annual leave, this increases by one day per year of service with the same employer.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
sentences.text: In 2022, over 90% of full-time resident employees aged 25 to 64 had more than seven days of annual leave.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
sentences.text: In addition, 64.6% of full-time resident employees aged 25 to 64 had 15 days or more of annual leave, higher than the 61.1% in 2018.

sections.label: No review of annual leave
sections.summary: Reviews of leave entitlements must consider business costs, and there are no plans to review annual leave entitlements now, though employers are encouraged to review benefits holistically.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
sentences.text: Besides employees' needs, reviews of leave entitlements must also take into account the impact on business costs.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Dr Koh Poh Koon) (for the Minister for Manpower)
sentences.text: There are no plans to review the annual leave entitlements for now, but we encourage more employers to review their employment benefits holistically to better attract and retain talent in our currently tight labour market.

sections.label: Leave, business costs and productivity
sections.summary: More leave may raise business costs through backfilling, but productivity can also come from training, job redesign, equipment, flexible work arrangements, skills and technology.

sentences.speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
sentences.text: The issue of giving more entitled leave and raising business costs is not something straightforward.

sentences.speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
sentences.text: But I think if you look at it from a very simplistic way: if more people do go on more leave, then the company's operations will require some backfilling, which may then require them to hire more extra people to backfill the persons who are on leave.

sentences.speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
sentences.text: So, in that more direct way, you can look at it as raising some form of business cost.

sentences.speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
sentences.text: But I think when we talk about being more productive, having more leave itself is not the only way to have people getting more rest and therefore becoming more productive.

sentences.speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
sentences.text: Productivity can come from many ways: through better training; better redesign of the job; and better equipment, for example, for those that need to perform manual tasks.

sentences.speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
sentences.text: We are looking at this from a more holistic way, by ensuring that there are avenues for other forms of work arrangements, including flexible work arrangements, and also equipping our workers with better skills and leveraging technology to be a multiplier of productivity.

sections.label: Minimum entitlement and lower-income workers
sections.summary: Increasing the minimum entitlement would help lower-income workers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
sentences.text: By increasing the minimum entitlement, it really would help our lower-income workers.
